 1                                             COMPLAINT

 2          Plaintiff Google LLC (“Google”), by and through its undersigned counsel, brings this

 3   action against Defendant NAO Tsargrad Media (“Tsargrad”) as set forth below:

 4                                     NATURE OF THE ACTION

 5          1.      Google brings this action to enjoin Tsargrad, a Russian entity subject to U.S.

 6   sanctions, from enforcing a Russian court judgment (the “Russian Judgment”) that Tsargrad

 7   obtained in breach of its contractual obligations to Google. The Russian Judgment imposes a) an

 8   order of specific performance on Google, demanding that Google and its affiliates provide

 9   Tsargrad with a Google account, YouTube channel and advertising services in violation of U.S.

10   law and/or Google’s policies, and b) a related financial penalty on Google and its affiliates for

11   not complying with the Russian court’s unconscionable order.

12          2.      Tsargrad obtained the Russian Judgment wrongfully—under a Russian law that

13   was passed to counter U.S. and other sanctions against Russia—and is now trying to enforce it in

14   foreign jurisdictions, causing further harm. Google seeks injunctive relief enjoining Tsargrad

15   from enforcing the Russian Judgment and all related appellate and other court decisions, as well

16   as declaratory relief that the Russian Judgment and all related appellate and other court decisions

17   are unenforceable against Google. Google’s request for relief has become particularly pressing as

18   it appears to have been served on August 2, 2024 with process in an enforcement action in

19   Turkey (the “Turkish Enforcement Action”).

20          3.      Google is a U.S. technology company that provides products and services to

21 users, including free services such as the search engine Google Search, the email platform

22 Gmail, and the video-sharing platform YouTube. Users with Google accounts can create

23 YouTube channels to upload content on YouTube, including videos, comments, and playlists.

24 They can enter into separate agreements to earn revenues, including from ad placements, on their

25 YouTube channels (“monetization”).

26          4.      Tsargrad is a Russian nationalist propaganda outlet indirectly majority-owned by

27 Konstantin Malofeyev, a Russian oligarch who has been sanctioned by the U.S. and other

28

       COMPLAINT
          Case 5:24-cv-05423-EJD Document 1 Filed 08/19/24 Page 3 of 21




 1   governments 1 for his role in funding Russia’s war in Ukraine, among other conduct. According

 2   to the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (“OFAC”),

 3   Malofeyev funded separatist activities in Eastern Ukraine, was a key source of financing for

 4   Russians promoting the annexation of Crimea, and supported pro-Russian activities that harm

 5   democracy, elections, and the security and stability of numerous countries. Tsargrad’s parent

 6   company, OOO Tsargrad, is owned by Malofeyev and has itself been sanctioned. 2 OFAC

 7   identified OOO Tsargrad as a “cornerstone” of Malofeyev’s “broad malign influence network”

 8   that “spreads pro-Kremlin propaganda and disinformation.” OOO Tsargrad spreads such

 9   propaganda and disinformation through Defendant.

10           5.      Tsargrad created a Google account, which was associated with the Gmail address

11   tsargradtv@gmail.com (the “Google Account”). In creating the Google Account, Tsargrad

12   agreed to Google’s Terms of Service (the “Google Terms of Service”). (Ex. A.) The Google

13   Terms of Service require all disputes arising out of or relating to the Google Terms of Service to

14   be resolved under California law in the courts of Santa Clara County, California. (Id. at 17.)

15 Tsargrad also created a YouTube channel under the YouTube Terms of Service (the “YouTube

16 Terms of Service”) and entered into a separate agreement with Google’s Irish affiliate, Google

17 Ireland Limited (“Google Ireland”), for advertising services (the “Monetization Contract”). The

18 YouTube Terms of Service and the Monetization Contract require all disputes arising out of or

19 relating to those contracts to be resolved under English law in the courts of England and Wales. 3

20           6.      In July 2020, Google ceased providing services to Tsargrad in compliance with

21   U.S. sanctions laws and/or Google’s relevant policies after identifying it as an entity that was

22   indirectly majority-owned by Malofeyev. Google terminated the Google Account and its

23   associated YouTube channel (the “YouTube Channel”). Google Ireland also ceased providing

24

   Zealand, Switzerland, Ukraine, and the United Kingdom.
26 2
     In addition, OFAC sanctioned OOO Tsargrad-Media “for being owned or controlled by, or for
27 having acted or purported to act for or on behalf of, directly or indirectly, [OOO] Tsargrad.”
   OOO Tsargrad-Media is an affiliate of Tsargrad. (See Ex. G.)

 1   advertising services to Tsargrad.

 2           7.     The Google Terms of Service required Tsargrad—which was subject to U.S.

 3   sanctions by virtue of Malofeyev’s majority ownership—to comply with sanctions laws. The

 4   Google Terms of Service also gave Google the right to terminate the Google Account, and

 5   thereby terminate the YouTube Channel, to comply with applicable law and Google’s policies.

 6   (Id. at 18.)

 7           8.     Notwithstanding the express language of the Google Terms of Service, Tsargrad

 8   sued Google in Russia, using a law that was specifically designed to counter U.S. and other

 9   foreign sanctions. (Ex. B.) Tsargrad alleged that the termination of the Google Account and the

10   YouTube Channel was improper. Tsargrad also sued Google Ireland under the Monetization

11   Contract and a Russian affiliate of Google, OOO Google (“Google Russia”), even though

12   Google Russia had no role in providing any services to Tsargrad and was not a counterparty to

13   the agreements with Tsargrad. Tsargrad thereby raised disputes relating to both the Google

14   Terms of Service and the YouTube Terms of Service in Russia, even though those Terms of

15   Service called for resolution of all disputes in, respectively, California and England.

16           9.     Tsargrad asked the Arbitrazh Court of the City of Moscow (the “Russian

17   Arbitrazh Court”), a civil trial court for business disputes, to order Google and its affiliates to

18   reinstate the Google Account and continue providing services to Tsargrad, in violation of U.S.

19   law and/or Google’s policies. Tsargrad further asked the Russian Arbitrazh Court to impose a

20   compounding penalty (called an “astreinte” under Russian law) on Google and its affiliates if the

21   account was not reinstated. Tsargrad asked that this penalty start at 100,000 rubles

22   (approximately $1,050) per day and double each week until Google complied with the Russian

23   Arbitrazh Court’s order.

24           10.    Even though the parties had expressly selected a forum outside Russia to resolve

25   disputes, the Russian Arbitrazh Court asserted jurisdiction—over Google’s objections—on the

26   grounds that Tsargrad was subject to sanctions that are “prescriptions of foreign authorities” that

27   are contrary to Russian public policy and should not apply to Russian entities. (Ex. C.)

28           11.    Google objected to jurisdiction and contested Tsargrad’s claims before the


       COMPLAINT                                        3
        Case 5:24-cv-05423-EJD Document 1 Filed 08/19/24 Page 5 of 21




 1   Russian Arbitrazh Court, to vindicate its agreed-upon rights to terminate contracts to comply

 2   with U.S. law and/or Google’s policies. These efforts were brushed aside by the Russian

 3   Arbitrazh Court, which issued a judgment on April 20, 2021 ordering Google and its affiliates to

 4   reinstate the Google Account and related services in violation of U.S. and other laws. (Ex. D.)

 5          12.     The Russian Judgment imposed Tsargrad’s requested penalty verbatim, holding

 6   that Google, Google Ireland and Google Russia were jointly and severally liable. In order to

 7   comply with U.S. law and/or Google’s policies, Google did not carry out the specific

 8   performance required by the Russian Judgment. As a result, this penalty continues to accrue

 9   unless and until the Google entities resume providing services to Tsargrad in violation of U.S.

10   law and/or Google’s policies. By issuing the Russian Judgment, the Russian courts demonstrated

11   that they are subject to political influence and have been weaponized to support Russia’s efforts

12   to undermine U.S. sanctions. As a result, the Russian Judgment is contrary to the international

13   legal order and subverts enforcement rules applicable in foreign jurisdictions, thereby

14   circumventing the policies and laws of local governments as enforced through their judicial

15   systems.

16          13.     In early March 2022, shortly after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Google

17   announced that it would pause the vast majority of its commercial activities in Russia, while also

18   confirming that its free services such as Search, Gmail, and YouTube were still operating there,

19   in an effort to provide users in Russia with access to information and an outlet for free

20   expression. Shortly thereafter, the Russian Federal Bailiff Service (the “Bailiffs”), an

21   instrumentality of the Russian government, seized Google Russia’s liquid assets to enforce the

22   Russian Judgment (the “Seizure”). The Bailiffs ordered Google Russia’s bank to freeze and

23   subsequently transfer all the money in Google Russia’s bank accounts to the Bailiffs on an

24   ongoing basis. The Bailiffs seized more than $100 million of Google Russia’s assets, even

25   though the amount purportedly due under the Judgment at the time was less than $12.5 million

26   (one billion rubles). Tsargrad received one billion rubles from the Seizure, which it said it would

27   use to support Russia’s war in Ukraine. As a result of the Seizure, Google Russia became

28   insolvent and is now undergoing liquidation. In addition to and separate from the Seizure, the


       COMPLAINT                                       4
          Case 5:24-cv-05423-EJD Document 1 Filed 08/19/24 Page 6 of 21




 1   compounding penalty under the Russian Judgment continues to accrue for Google.

 2           14.     Tsargrad recently initiated the Turkish Enforcement Action, seeking to enforce

 3   the Russian Judgment and related appellate and other court decisions, including a decision by the

 4   Ninth Arbitrazh Court of Appeal (the “Russian Appellate Court”), a civil appellate court,

 5   affirming the Russian Judgment and an additional decision by the Russian Arbitrazh Court in

 6   Google Russia’s bankruptcy proceedings issued on the basis of the Russian Judgment, against

 7   Google, Google Ireland, and Google Russia. (Ex. E.) Tsargrad appears to have served Google

 8   with process under the Hague Service Convention on August 2, 2024. The Turkish Enforcement

 9   Action is an attempt to seize funds from Google for complying with sanctions against Russian

10   entities.

11           15.     On information and belief, Tsargrad plans to bring more enforcement actions in

12   additional countries around the world. According to public reporting, Tsargrad and two other

13   Russian astreinte holders 4 plan to enforce the Russian Judgment in fifteen foreign jurisdictions,

14   which will cause Google further harm in contravention of the binding provisions of the Google

15   Terms of Service and the YouTube Terms of Service. 5 In addition, Tsargrad may file a lawsuit in

16   Russia under a Russian law that was passed to counter the impact of sanctions, seeking an

17   injunction to prevent Google from proceeding with this action (an “anti-suit injunction”).

18           16.     Google, an American company headquartered in this district, seeks expedited,

19   equitable relief from this Court including, inter alia:

20        ● injunctive relief enjoining enforcement of the Russian Judgment and all related appellate

21           and other court decisions outside Russia;

22        ● injunctive relief enjoining Tsargrad’s efforts to obtain an anti-suit injunction in Russia

23

24
     4
     Google is filing complaints against these two other companies, ANO TV-Novosti and NO Fond
25 Pravoslavnogo Televideniya, also seeking temporary restraining orders and preliminary
   injunctive relief. Google intends to file an Administrative Motion to Relate the three cases

   because “[i]t appears likely that there will be an unduly burdensome duplication of labor and

   Rule 3-12(a)(2).

   (June 11, 2024), https://pravo.ru/news/253511/?_x_tr_hist=true.

        Case 5:24-cv-05423-EJD Document 1 Filed 08/19/24 Page 7 of 21




 1           relating to this lawsuit;

 2       ● declaratory relief that the forum-selection clause and choice-of-law provisions of the

 3           Google Terms of Service are valid and binding upon the parties; and

 4       ● declaratory relief that Tsargrad breached the Google Terms of Service when it filed its

 5           lawsuit in Russia in an attempt to force Google to violate U.S. sanctions laws and/or its

 6           own policies.

 7           17.     California strongly favors enforcing presumptively valid forum-selection clauses

 8   and Google—which was wrongfully sued by Tsargrad in Russia because Google complied with

 9   U.S. sanctions—seeks protection under the laws of California, which the parties agreed would

10   govern any dispute arising under the Google Terms of Service.

11                                                PARTIES

12           18.     Plaintiff Google is a Delaware limited liability company with its principal place of

13   business in Mountain View, California.

14           19.     Defendant Tsargrad is a Russian media company organized under Russian law

15   with its principal place of business in Russia. Tsargrad is indirectly majority-owned by the

16   Russian oligarch Konstantin Malofeyev. Both Malofeyev and Tsargrad’s parent company, OOO

17   Tsargrad, have been designated by OFAC as Specially Designated Nationals (“SDNs”) subject to

18   U.S. sanctions. According to OFAC, “Malofeyev, covertly or through intermediaries, supported

19   pro-Russian activities that undermine democracy, interfere in elections, and degrade security and

20   stability in a host of countries.”

21                                        JURISDICTION & VENUE

22           20.     This Court has personal jurisdiction over Tsargrad because Tsargrad agreed to be

23   subject to suit in this Court. Tsargrad agreed to the Google Terms of Service, which state (in

24   relevant part) that, “All disputes in any way relating to these terms, the additional terms of use of

25   individual services, or the services, regardless of conflict of laws rules, shall be resolved in

26   accordance with the laws of the State of California, USA. Such disputes are subject to the

27   exclusive jurisdiction of the federal and state courts located in Santa Clara County,

28   California, USA.” (Ex. A at 17 (emphasis added).)


       COMPLAINT                                        6
        Case 5:24-cv-05423-EJD Document 1 Filed 08/19/24 Page 8 of 21




 1             21.   To the extent necessary, Tsargrad also has sufficient minimum contacts with

 2   California because Tsargrad—through its litigation in Russia and in Turkey—seeks to cause

 3   Google, a citizen of California, to take action within California to comply with the Russian

 4   Judgment.

 5             22.   This Court has subject matter jurisdiction over this action pursuant to 28 U.S.C.

 6   § 1332(a)(2). The amount in controversy exceeds $75,000, exclusive of interest and costs.

 7   Google is a citizen of California and Delaware, while Tsargrad is a citizen of a foreign state,

 8   Russia.

 9             23.   Venue is proper in the United States District Court for the Northern District of

10 California under 28 U.S.C. 1391(b) because the Google Terms of Service provide that “All

11 disputes in any way relating to these terms . . . are subject to the exclusive jurisdiction of the

12   federal and state courts located in Santa Clara County, California, USA” (Id. at 17), and the

13   parties expressly consented to personal jurisdiction in these courts.

14                                      FACTUAL BACKGROUND

15             A.    Tsargrad Creates the Google Account and Agrees to the Google Terms of

16                   Service

17             24.   In August 2014, Tsargrad created the Google Account, which was associated with

18   the Gmail address tsargradtv@gmail.com, and the YouTube Channel, which was associated with

19   the Google Account.

20             25.   In creating the Google Account, Tsargrad agreed to the Google Terms of Service.

21   Under the Google Terms of Service, Tsargrad agreed to updates to the Google Terms of Service

22   as a condition of maintaining the Google Account. (Id. at 19.)

23             26.   At all relevant times, the Google Terms of Service gave Google the right to

24   terminate the Google Account if (among other things) Tsargrad’s use of the Google Account

25   violated applicable laws or the Google Terms of Service. (Id. at 17.) The Google Terms of

26   Service as modified provided that “Google reserves the right to temporarily or permanently

27   block your access to services or delete your Google account” if “you materially or repeatedly

28   breach these terms, additional terms, or the rules applicable to individual services” or if “this is


       COMPLAINT                                       7
        Case 5:24-cv-05423-EJD Document 1 Filed 08/19/24 Page 9 of 21




 1   required to comply with a legal requirement or a court order.” (Id.)

 2          27.     In addition, at all relevant times, the Google Terms of Service contained a binding

 3   choice-of-law and forum-selection clause, which stated:

 4                  All disputes in any way relating to these terms, the additional terms

 5                  of use of individual services or the services, regardless of conflict

 6                  of laws rules, shall be resolved in accordance with the laws of the

 7                  State of California, USA. Such disputes are subject to the

 8                  exclusive jurisdiction of the federal and state courts located in

 9                  Santa Clara County, California, USA.

10   (Id. at 17 (emphasis added).)

11          B.      Google Exercises its Contractual Right to Cease Providing Services to

12                  Tsargrad due to OFAC Sanctions

13          28.     OFAC and the U.S. Department of State have the authority to designate entities

14   and individuals that engage in activities contrary to U.S. foreign policy or national security as

15   SDNs. Under U.S. law, U.S. persons may not engage in dealings, directly or indirectly, with any

16   party either (i) expressly designated an SDN by OFAC or the State Department, or (ii) owned

17   50% or more by an SDN.

18          29.     In July 2020, Google and Google Ireland ceased providing services to Tsargrad in

19   compliance with U.S. sanctions laws and/or Google’s relevant policies, after determining that

20   Tsargrad had created the Google Account and YouTube Channel and that it was indirectly

21   majority-owned by Malofeyev, who had been designated by OFAC as an SDN. Google

22   terminated the Google Account and YouTube Channel, which had the effect of terminating

23   services provided in connection with that account. Google Ireland similarly stopped providing

24   advertising services to Tsargrad.

25          C.      Tsargrad Files Suit in Russia, Breaching the Google Terms of Service

26          30.     Even though Google terminated the Google Account to comply with U.S. law and

27   Google’s policies, and Google was entitled to do so under the Google Terms of Service,

28   Tsargrad still demanded that the Google Account and related services be reinstated. Instead of


       COMPLAINT                                       8
          Case 5:24-cv-05423-EJD Document 1 Filed 08/19/24 Page 10 of 21




 1   raising this dispute in California, as required by the explicit terms of the Google Terms of

 2   Service, on August 27, 2020, Tsargrad sued Google in the Russian Arbitrazh Court. (Ex. B.) By

 3   bringing its litigation in Russia, Tsargrad breached the Google Terms of Service.

 4           31.     Tsargrad asked the Russian Arbitrazh Court for an order requiring Google to

 5   reinstate the Google Account and related services. (Id. at 9.) Tsargrad also improperly named

 6   Google Russia as a defendant, even though Google Russia had no contractual relationship with

 7   Tsargrad, did not provide the Google Account or any related services, and did not have the legal

 8   or technical ability to restore the Google Account. (See id. at 1.)

 9           32.     Tsargrad claimed its suit was permissible under Article 248.1 of the Arbitrazh

10   Procedural Code of the Russian Federation (the “APC”), introduced by Russian Law No. 171-FZ

11   (hereinafter, “Article 248.1”). (Ex. F.) Article 248.1 was enacted by Russia in June 2020 to

12   counter the impact of sanctions from “unfriendly foreign states,” including the U.S., and purports

13   to grant Russian courts “exclusive jurisdiction” over disputes involving Russian individuals

14   subject to sanctions by foreign states, “unless otherwise provided by . . . agreement of the

15   parties.” (Id. at 1.) The Google Terms of Service constitute such an agreement, as they provide

16   that disputes between Tsargrad and Google will be heard in the courts of Santa Clara County,

17   California. And while the Google Terms of Service permit account holders to petition foreign

18   courts only “if applicable local law prevents certain disputes from being resolved in a California

19   court” or “if applicable local law prevents [a user’s] local court from applying California law to

20   resolve these disputes,” (Ex. A at 18 (emphases added)), Article 248.1 does not “prevent”

21   Tsargrad from complying with the Google Terms of Service’s forum-selection clause. Instead,

22   Article 248.1 is permissive, rather than mandatory. It gives sanctioned Russian parties the option

23   of proceeding in Russia, but does not require them to do so. Indeed, other sanctioned Russian

24 parties have appeared in U.S. courts since. 6

25
     6
       See, e.g., Schansman et al v. Sberbank of Russia PJSC et al., No. 1:19-cv-02985-ALC-GWG,
26
     S.D.N.Y., ECF Nos. 396–400 (notices of appearance dated July 13, 2022 on behalf of Sberbank
27   of Russia, a sanctioned Russian entity which was designated by OFAC on February 24, 2022);
     id., ECF Nos. 426–28 (notices of appearance dated August 30, 2022 and August 31, 2022 on
28   behalf of VTB Bank, a sanctioned Russian entity which was also designated on February 24,
     2022).
         COMPLAINT                                     9
       Case 5:24-cv-05423-EJD Document 1 Filed 08/19/24 Page 11 of 21




 1          33.     Nonetheless, the Russian Arbitrazh Court ignored the forum-selection and choice-

 2   of-law provisions in the Google Terms of Service, accepted Tsargrad’s arguments, and asserted

 3   jurisdiction to hear the case under Article 248.1. (Ex. C at 3.) Google objected to the jurisdiction

 4   of the Russian courts. The Russian Arbitrazh Court wholly disregarded the parties’ agreement to

 5   resolve all disputes in the courts of Santa Clara County, California, misapplied the law, and did

 6   not afford Google due process. The Russian Arbitrazh Court, among other things, ignored the

 7   corporate distinction between Google and Google Russia—a distinct entity and one that had

 8   assets in the jurisdiction—without any factual or legitimate legal basis, thereby allowing

 9   Tsargrad to seize Google Russia’s assets. The Russian Arbitrazh Court determined that the

10   Russian stance against U.S. sanctions overrode the terms of the parties’ explicit agreement and

11   the domestic law applicable to the parties and ignored valid legal and factual defenses Google

12   raised. Without waiving its jurisdictional objection, Google was forced to litigate the case to

13   judgment before the Russian Arbitrazh Court in an effort to mitigate damages.

14          34.     In April 2021, the Russian Arbitrazh Court found in favor of Tsargrad on the

15   merits of its claims and ordered Google to reinstate the Google Account and related services,

16   including the YouTube Channel. (Ex. D.) The court adopted Tsargrad’s request verbatim and

17   imposed a compounding penalty in the amount of 100,000 rubles for each day of non-

18   performance, starting from the sixth day from the effective date of the judgment, subject to a

19   weekly twofold increase of the amount of the daily penalty. (Id. at 6, 8.) The court identified the

20   penalty as an “astreinte” and stated that it would run until the defendants complied with its order

21 for specific performance, which would require Google to violate applicable U.S. law. (Id. at 7.)

22   The Russian Appellate Court affirmed the Russian Judgment, subject to imposing a cap on the

23   astreinte for a nine-month period of one billion rubles, after which it would start to accrue again.

24   The Supreme Court of Russia summarily upheld the Russian Judgment as modified by the

25   Russian Appellate Court.

26          35.     In January 2022, Google temporarily restored the Google Account, after obtaining

27   a license from OFAC that allowed Google to do so. By taking these actions, Google made a

28   concerted effort to comply with the Russian Judgment. The Google Account’s restoration


       COMPLAINT                                      10
       Case 5:24-cv-05423-EJD Document 1 Filed 08/19/24 Page 12 of 21




 1   permitted access to the YouTube Channel so it could be used within Russia while being

 2   geographically blocked from viewers outside the country. The OFAC license did not authorize

 3   provision of monetization services, and Google Ireland did not reinstate services under the

 4   Monetization Contract. Google also did not pay the astreinte. Therefore, Google did the best it

 5 could to respond to the Russian court’s impossible judgment while complying with U.S. law and

 6 Google’s policies. Nonetheless, the Russian Arbitrazh Court held that Google had not complied

 7 with its judgment. This belied the idea that the Russian Judgment’s objective was to ensure

 8 Tsargrad regained the use of the Google Account and the YouTube Channel, rather than to

 9 punish Google for complying with U.S. sanctions.

10          36.     After its OFAC license expired, Google again terminated the Google Account and

11 associated services to comply with U.S. law and/or Google’s policies.

12          D.      Enforcement of the Russian Judgment Leads to Liquidation of Google

13                  Russia

14          37.     Tsargrad first enforced the Russian Judgment against Google Russia.

15          38.     In early March 2022, after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, Google announced that it

16 would pause the vast majority of its commercial activities in Russia, while maintaining the

17 operation of free services such as Search, Gmail, and YouTube, to provide Russian users with

18 access to information and an outlet for free expression.

19          39.     Shortly thereafter, the Bailiffs enforced the Russian Judgment by seizing all of

20 Google Russia’s liquid assets. The Bailiffs ordered Google Russia’s bank to freeze and

21 subsequently transfer all the money in Google Russia’s accounts to the Bailiffs on an ongoing
